back: Both 'will' and 'be going to' can often be used for planned events.
We prefer 'will' for predictions based on experience or opinion.
We prefer 'be going to' when there is present evidence (e.g., 'the sky's gone dark').

front: I bet, I expect, I hope
back: These introductory phrases usually collocate with 'will'.
Use 'will' when making a decision right now (e.g., 'I'll pick him up').
Use 'be going to' for decisions already made.
In formal notices, 'will' is preferred for arranged future events.
Use 'will' or 'be going to' with little difference in meaning in the main clause.
Use 'will' when one thing is the inevitable result of another.
is going to have (based on evidence).

front: Ex 9.1 (10b): She ... better with some fresh air.

back: Use 'will', not 'be going to', for offers and promises.
If you look left, you will see the lake (expecting ability).

front: Ex 9.2 (1): I ... how the equipment works.

back: There is going to be a storm (present evidence).
